title: Learning chords and playing like Benny Goodman and Lionel Hampton
summary: He explains the chord lessons, ninth chords, and learning from visiting big bands.

bands.name: Clyde Kerr and William Houston's band

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Oh the trumpet. Yeah. See, where that story is, there's a garage there now. But what I mean, I used to play up on a TikTok up there with, see Clyde Kerr and William Houston had a band up there, and Poirier bought them uniforms and everything, and when I won all them contests and everything, well I never had nobody to book me, if I could have got somebody to book me. Because Lewis Jordan was coming out then with that stuff, with his temperament fire, well I had outfits something like that better than what he had, because we could play what he's playing and we was playing on the order of Benny Goodman and you know, I mean Lionel Hampton and all that kind of stuff. You see, we was rippin' and playing all types of music. Anything come out because a lot of them guys would catch it off the records and things like that and we'd get them riffs and we'd kill the, you know him, he used to write for us too, the trumpet press. Now Killde, when I got on banjo, or off of banjo, he made me get a board and draw the finger board of a guitar. And made me learn every string on and every fret on and you see it's a lot of stuff can be made on a piano where you can't make it on a guitar because the lowest you make on a banjo guitar is F and you can make a G or something on a piano, you see. Well I would, he showed me how to break up all them chords, you know, chords to use a C, C, just like a ninth chord or something like that. Well a banjo, you can make them but they're not complete with a banjo. Well a guitar, you can make them complete on a guitar, you see. It's nothing but a ninth chord, it's just like a seven, like take the chord of C, C, E and G, well that would be the triad and you add the seven to C, E understand, which would be B-flat, well that would be the dominant seven or the major seven would be B-natural. Well you add the ninth to it would be D, you understand what I mean? You understand, add A to it that would be six, the six of them. Well I mean we used to have all them drill and studs and the groups that we would have would make everybody learn chords and different things like that because sometimes a guy would be playing, we would try to catch the chord and tell him what chord to make, well he'd know what he was talking about. But if he didn't know the chord he couldn't, he'd be like he was talking to China to him, you understand? So at that weight we learned all that kind of stuff.
What's the band you play with?

Yeah, Red played or I'd live too. Well I mean we played by air or whatever you might call it. Because some of them groups now you take like Coo Coo and George Lewis and them, well they come back playing music again after Shark and them brought them back when they started Dixieland back on Boyleville Street. But you see them fellas, when we was ridin' all that hell around there with these bands, and when I was at Chinatown, you had Louis Primer used to be there every night, you understand? And all them big bands like Oiskin, Hawkins, all of them out of town used to come in and Shark and Banana, you used to have prize fights at the Coliseum on Friday night, and all them prize fighters. Charlie Barnett like, guy used that Cherokee for a theme song, all that boys used to come in and sit in with us and we'd steal from them, they'd want to play you and show you how, you know, different things like that. So we was always learning something.
